clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 60s presented with decompensated metabolic syndrome, refractory arterial hypertension, significant weight gain, and psychiatric symptoms. Initial workup included abdominal imaging, which revealed a large bilobed left adrenal mass. Hormonal studies showed marginally increased DHEAS and urinary catecholamines, while other adrenal hormones were normal. The mass was surgically resected, and subsequent histology confirmed an oncocytic adrenocortical carcinoma, staged as pT2 pN0 R1, with incomplete resection (R1), and fulfilling the Lin-Weiss-Bisceglia criteria for malignant ACONs.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with symptoms including refractory arterial hypertension, weight gain, dizziness, headache, asthenia, psychotic breakdown, anxiety, hypokalemia, and hypernatremia, suggestive of adrenal dysfunction.
Abdominal CT imaging confirmed a bilobed left adrenal mass, measuring 8x5 cm and 1.8x2.2 cm, which was vascularized without calcifications, and ruled out locoregional or distant spreading.

Hormonal assessment showed normal estradiol, progesterone, 17-OH-progesterone, androstenedione, and cortisoluria, but marginally increased DHEAS (9.17 µmol/L) and urinary catecholamines (metanephrine 1283 nmol/24 hours, normetanephrine 4218 nmol/24 hours, methoxytyramine 2107 nmol/24 hours).
Subsequent histology results revealed an oncocytic adrenocortical carcinoma, staged as pT2 pN0 R1, with incomplete resection on the non-peritonealised side (R1).
The mass fulfilled the Lin-Weiss-Bisceglia criteria for malignant ACONs.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Classic Cushing's Syndrome due to cortisol-producing adenoma
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Cortisoluria was normal, and other classic markers of hypercortisolism were not elevated (E005).

While urinary catecholamines were marginally increased, the primary diagnosis was adrenocortical carcinoma based on histology, and the clinical picture was more consistent with hypercortisolism/androgen excess rather than a classic pheochromocytoma crisis.
